title: The Selfish Giant
text:
Every afternoon after school the children played in the Giant's garden. It was large and lovely, with soft grass, flowers like stars and twelve peach trees. Then the Giant came home from a seven-year visit to his friend the Cornish ogre. Seeing the children, he shouted them away, built a high wall around the garden and put up a sign: Trespassers Will Be Prosecuted.

Spring came to the rest of the country, but not to the Giant's garden. Snow and Frost moved in, the North Wind came to stay, and the Hail rattled on the roof. Summer and autumn passed it by.

One morning the Giant heard a bird singing. The children had crept in through a hole in the wall, and in every tree sat a child, and the trees had burst into blossom. Only in one corner was it still winter, where a tiny boy stood crying because he could not reach the branches. The Giant's heart melted. He went down, lifted the boy into the tree, which flowered at once, and the boy kissed him. The Giant knocked down the wall and gave the garden to the children.

The little boy never came back, though the Giant longed for him. Years later, when the Giant was old, he saw him one winter morning under a tree white with blossom, with the marks of nails in his hands and feet. "You let me play once in your garden," the child said. "Today you shall come with me to my garden, which is Paradise." That afternoon the children found the Giant lying dead under the tree, covered with white blossoms.
lesson: Closing yourself off from others to protect what is yours leaves your life cold. Opening your door is what lets things grow.
people: The Giant, the children, a little boy
source: Oscar Wilde, The Selfish Giant, in The Happy Prince and Other Tales (1888)
